info.title: go-time-recording API
info.description:
Project time tracking.

Authenticate either with the session cookie obtained from `POST /auth/login`, or with a personal API token sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-API-Token: <token>`.

A token carries no rights of its own: every request is evaluated against the owner's **current** role, so changing or revoking a role takes effect on the very next call.

All responses are wrapped by the framework as `{"data": ...}` on success and `{"error": {"message": ...}}` on failure.

tags.name: auth
tags.description: Sign-in, sign-out and your own account

post.summary: Sign in

totp.description: Required when the account has two-factor authentication enabled.

201.description: Signed in; a session cookie is set. When the response says `totpRequired`, no cookie is set and the code must be supplied.

get.summary: Whether passkeys can be used on this connection
get.description: Browsers expose WebAuthn only on a secure context - HTTPS, or localhost - and reject an IP address as a relying party identifier. The interface asks before offering a button that could only fail with "SecurityError: This is an invalid domain".

post.summary: Start a passwordless sign-in
post.description: Returns a challenge. No username is asked for: the browser offers whichever credentials it holds for this site, and the one that signs names its own owner.

put.summary: Finish a passwordless sign-in
put.description: Verifies the signature and opens a session, exactly as a password sign-in does - same cookie, same lifetime, same CSRF rotation. Every failure answers alike.

get.summary: Whether a Kerberos sign-in is on offer
get.description: True where a keytab was read at start and a directory is configured to look a ticket's owner up in. The interface asks before trying one, so a browser on an installation without either is never sent the Negotiate challenge.

post.summary: Sign in with a Kerberos ticket
post.description: The ticket travels as `Authorization: Negotiate …`, which a browser sends by itself once it trusts this address; a request without one is answered 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate`, the challenge that asks for it. Only a ticket of the keytab's realm is accepted. Its owner is looked up in the directory - as named, then as name@REALM - and signed in to the account a directory password sign-in reaches, with the same session, cookie and CSRF rotation. A second factor the account holds is asked for with `totpRequired`, and the code is sent back as `totp` with the ticket.

totp.description: Required when the account has two-factor authentication enabled.

201.description: Signed in; a session cookie is set. When the response says `totpRequired`, no cookie is set and the code must be supplied.

401.description: No ticket, a ticket that does not verify, or an owner the directory does not hold. Without a ticket the answer carries `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate`.

409.description: No keytab was read at start (`kerberosOff`), or no directory is configured to look a ticket's owner up in (`kerberosNeedsDirectory`).

post.summary: Sign out and end the session

get.summary: The signed-in user and their permissions

put.summary: Change your own password; ends every session you have

400.description: Wrong current password, or the new one is too short

put.summary: Set your interface language
Set the appearance you read in, or clear it to follow the time of day
put.description: "light", "dark", or an empty value. Empty is meaningful rather than an omission: it is how somebody goes back to the screen following the time of day. The appearance is stored on the account rather than in the browser, so a shared machine does not hand the next person the last one's.

get.description: Answers {"region": "", "instanceRegion": "BY", "effectiveRegion": "BY", "regions": ["BW", ...]}. region is your own choice: empty follows the installation, "none" keeps no holidays at all, and a German state by its ISO 3166-2 code without the country (BW, BY, BE, BB, HB, HH, HE, MV, NI, NW, RP, SL, SN, ST, SH, TH) keeps that state's. effectiveRegion is what applies, empty for none. A state's holidays are those that hold in the whole of it; one that holds only where you work is recorded as an absence of the kind localHoliday.

put.summary: Choose whose public holidays you keep
put.description: Body: {"region": "HH"} - a state, "none", or empty to follow the installation again.

put.summary: Set your own timezone, or clear it to follow the instance
put.description: An IANA name such as "Europe/Berlin". An empty value is meaningful: it clears the personal setting so the account follows the instance-wide zone again. An unknown name is rejected rather than stored, because it would otherwise fall back to UTC at every use and move bookings between days.

put.summary: Record whether you have been shown the guided tour
put.description: Stored on the user rather than in the browser, so someone who has been introduced to the application is not introduced again on their next device. Settable both ways: sending false offers the tour again, which is how the "Show the tour" button works.

get.description: Carries no key material. The public half could be sent harmlessly - it verifies signatures and cannot produce them - but sending it invites building something on a value that is meaningless outside a ceremony. `createdAt` and `lastUsedAt` are RFC 3339 moments rather than dates, for the reason the token listing gives.

post.summary: Start registering a passkey
post.description: Refused for the built-in administrator: it is the guaranteed way back into an installation, and a guarantee that depends on a particular device still existing is not one.

put.summary: Finish registering a passkey
put.description: Verifies what the authenticator created and stores the public half.

delete.description: Scoped to the owner, so an id from somewhere else deletes nothing. Allowed even for the last one: a passkey is an addition to the password, never a replacement, so removing it cannot lock anyone out.

post.summary: Begin two-factor enrolment; the secret is returned once

put.summary: Confirm two-factor with a current code

get.summary: List your API tokens; secrets are never returned
get.description: `createdAt`, `expiresAt` and `lastUsedAt` are RFC 3339 moments, not dates. They used to be days, which is the wrong answer for the field somebody reads when they think a token has been taken: a token used at three in the morning read exactly like one used at three in the afternoon, and one used twice today read as used once. A use is written down at most once a minute, so `lastUsedAt` can be up to a minute behind the latest one.

post.summary: Issue an API token; the secret is shown once and cannot be recovered

expiresInDays.description: 0 means the token does not expire on its own.

409.description: Token limit reached

delete.summary: Revoke one of your own tokens

get.description: Your own entries, one page at a time. `userId` may name you, which is a reasonable thing for a client to send; naming anybody else is refused rather than quietly answered with your own rows, because a list that does not match what was asked for is worse than a plain no. A request naming no `limit` gets the default page rather than every entry you have ever booked, and `totalCount` is how many match altogether - so a page shorter than `totalCount` means there is another one. For the same reason a `limit` above the maximum is refused rather than reduced.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Only the entries whose description contains this text, whatever its case. Matched as written: a percent sign or an underscore is a character, not a wildcard. On SQLite only ASCII letters are folded, so there `Ä` does not find `ä`. Longer than a description can be (2000 characters) is refused.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Entries per page. Default 100, maximum 500; above that the request is refused.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: How many matching entries to skip. Only meaningful with a stable order, which this listing has: newest day first, ties broken by id.

post.summary: Book time
post.description: `projectId` is optional; omitting it records uncategorised hours. Omitting `userId` books for the caller.

409.description: Daily limit exceeded, or the project no longer accepts entries

put.summary: Update an entry
put.description: Changes an entry of your own. Somebody else’s answers 404, exactly as an id nobody holds does, so the answer does not say which ids are real - on every method, not only here. Naming somebody else in `userId`, which would hand the entry over, is refused, and there is no right that changes either. A project given here goes through the same checks as booking onto it: it must exist, be one you may see, and still accept hours. Every field is optional: one left out or sent as null stays as it is - null does not remove anything here. A `projectId` of 0 takes the entry off its project, and an empty `description` empties it.

409.description: The day would go over its ceiling, or the project no longer accepts hours

post.summary: Move an entry to another project

409.description: The entry is already on that project, or the project is closed for booking

get.description: Your own projects, which is all there are. There were two kinds - a shared project everybody could see and a private category - and a `private=true` parameter to narrow to the latter; every project belongs to one person now, so there is nothing to narrow. Each carries budgetHours - how many hours you mean to spend on it, null for none - and bookedHours, how many of your own are booked on it. Needs `projects:read`.

post.summary: Create a project
post.description: The project belongs to whoever created it, always. There was a `private: true` to ask for that, and `projects:write:own` beside `projects:write` to decide which kind you were allowed to make; there is one kind, so neither is left. `startDate` is optional - a project is one person’s way of organising their own hours, not a plan. `budgetHours` is optional too: how many hours you mean to spend on it, between 0 and 100000, which nobody but you sees or signs off. Needs `projects:write`.

404.description: Unknown, or not yours - which answers the same way, so asking cannot tell you what colleagues have

put.summary: Update a project
put.description: Changes a project of your own. Every field is optional: one left out or sent as null stays as it is - null does not remove anything here. An empty `endDate` takes the end date off, an empty `description` empties it, and a `budgetHours` of 0 takes the budget off.

409.description: The project still has time entries

post.summary: Archive a completed project

409.description: Not completed, or open entries remain

get.description: Your own hours on the project, and nobody else’s. It used to be a breakdown per colleague, gated on a separate `reports:read` that no role held, so the screen was unreachable and would have shown what each colleague had booked. Needs `reports:read:own`.

get.summary: Hours you booked, with or without a project
get.description: Your own hours over a period. `projectId` chooses what it covers: leave it out for every project, send `none` for the hours that were never given one, or send an id for that project. The project-scoped report at `/projects/{id}/report` cannot express either of the first two, because an id has no spare value for "all" and "none" at once. Needs `reports:read:own`.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: A project id, `none` for the entries without a project, or omitted for all.

400.description: Unreadable project selection, or a range that ends before it starts

get.description: Your own balance, which needs `reports:read:own`. Anyone else’s is refused outright: a balance is their recorded time, totalled, and nobody reads that. Which days count depends on everyDayCountsFrom (see /users/{id}/working-times). Without it, and before it, only days with bookings count, each measured against the week in force on it (see /me/schedules) - without a plan, the daily target from Monday to Friday and nothing at the weekend. From it on, every working day up to today counts, booked or not, and asks what its week plans less what a public holiday (see /me/holidays) or an absence (see /me/absences) takes off it: nothing on a holiday, a day of leave, a sick day or a local holiday, half on half a day of leave, the whole day on a day off against overtime. A day after today counts once something is booked on it. Each day says why it asks less where something does, as absence or holiday, and the answer carries everyDayCountsFrom, null while only booked days count.

post.summary: Create a user

409.description: Email already in use

get.summary: Read a user; your own account needs no permission

put.summary: Update a user

409.description: The built-in administrator cannot be deleted

put.summary: Assign a role

409.description: The built-in administrator must keep a role that can administer

put.summary: Reset an account password
put.description: Gives an account a password chosen by whoever holds users:write, for letting somebody back in who has forgotten theirs. The account is flagged to replace it before it can use anything, and every session it has open ends. Refused for the caller’s own account, which is changed through /me/password with the current password, and for a directory account, whose password lives in the directory.

409.description: Your own account, or one kept in the directory

put.summary: Set your own daily target and daily maximum

400.description: The target cannot exceed the maximum

403.description: Somebody else's account, or the right is not held

put.description: Yours alone. Needs `settings:write:own`, and the id has to be your own: there is no wider permission that reaches somebody else’s, because a daily target is a time figure and everything to do with time belongs to the person it is about. An empty value, sent as 0, means "follow the instance default" under Settings. everyDayCountsFrom (YYYY-MM-DD) is the day from which every working day counts towards your balance, booked or not; absent leaves it alone, and an empty string takes it off again, so only booked days count, as they did before you chose one. The account that administers this installation cannot set these for anybody, which is deliberate - it cannot read the entries, the balance or the figures the numbers produce.

post.summary: Create a role
post.description: A role has to grant at least one permission: one that grants nothing can be assigned, and whoever holds it signs in to an interface with nothing on it.

put.summary: Update a role

409.description: System roles cannot be renamed or weakened

put.description: A system role may be described differently and nothing else: not renamed, and its permissions not changed in either direction. That role belongs to the built-in administrator, which configures the installation and records no time — a right added here would hand it a working day from the screen that administers roles. Somebody who should both work here and administer is given the user-admin role instead.

409.description: System role, or the role is still assigned

get.description: Public on purpose: the sign-in screen needs it before anyone is authenticated.

put.summary: Save branding

get.summary: What a fresh installation still has to settle
get.description: Each step reports whether it is done, worked out from what is actually configured rather than from a record of the wizard having been shown - so a setting that is undone makes its step outstanding again. Two steps are required (the administrator password and the timezone); the rest are optional. Built-in administrator only, because a list of what is not yet configured is a useful thing for an attacker to read. Deliberately reachable while the initial password blocks the rest of the API.

post.summary: Dismiss the wizard
post.description: Records that the wizard was dismissed, which settles the optional steps only. It reappears by itself while any required step is outstanding, so this cannot be used to run an installation without a timezone.

post.summary: Claim the session the installer earned
post.description: Answered before anybody is signed in, and only on a process that actually served an installer. The browser holding that installer’s setup token is given a session for the built-in administrator, so the first screen after the installation is the one asking for a password rather than one asking for the documented initial password. Refused once a password has been chosen, and refused entirely on an installation configured without the installer.

parameters.name: X-Setup-Token
parameters.description: The token the installer printed to this process’s log.

409.description: No installer ran, or the installation has already been taken into use

get.description: Returns three things: the values an administrator has overridden, the values currently in force, and the values the configuration file supplies. An absent field under "configured" means that limit still follows the file.

put.summary: Set the operational limits
put.description: Send only the fields to override; omitting one makes it follow the configuration file again, and an empty object resets everything. Values are bounded on save, because this screen can otherwise lock out its own administrator. Takes effect within seconds, without a restart. Administrator only.

get.description: Answers {"region": "BY", "regions": ["BW", ...]}: the German state whose public holidays everybody keeps who has not chosen their own, or empty for none - which is what an installation that never chose one keeps. For whoever administers the installation.

put.summary: Choose the installation's public holidays
put.description: Body: {"region": "BY"} - a state by its ISO 3166-2 code without the country (BW, BY, BE, BB, HB, HH, HE, MV, NI, NW, RP, SL, SN, ST, SH, TH), or empty for none.

put.summary: Set the instance-wide timezone
put.description: Decides which calendar day a booking falls on for every user who has not set their own. Administrator only.

get.summary: Read the stored database connection; the password is never returned

put.summary: Save the database connection; applied on the next restart
put.description: An empty password keeps the one in force, and only for the same type, host, port and user: a connection naming another server or user is sent no password it was not given.

get.summary: Read the logging, metrics and tracing settings
get.description: Returns what has been administered under "configured" and what this process is actually writing, serving and exporting under "active". The two disagree until the next restart. An absent field under "configured" follows the configuration file; "traceExporter": "" is an administered off, which is a different thing. Administrator only.

put.summary: Set the logging, metrics and tracing settings; applied on the next restart
put.description: Send only the fields to administer; an empty object makes everything follow the configuration file again. "logLevel" is DEBUG, INFO, NOTICE, WARN, ERROR or FATAL. "traceExporter" is "otlp", "jaeger" or "" for off, and needs "tracerUrl" as host:port when it names an exporter, with https:// in front to encrypt the export or http:// or nothing for plaintext - another scheme or a path is refused, because the exporter speaks OTLP over gRPC. "metricsOff": true stops the metrics endpoint being served; the port itself stays in the configuration file, because GoFr refuses to start when something already holds it. The log level takes effect on the next line written; the rest is applied when the application is restarted, because GoFr binds the port and builds the exporter while starting up. Administrator only.

post.summary: Probe a database connection without saving or switching to it
post.description: An empty password keeps the one in force, and only for the same type, host, port and user: a connection naming another server or user is sent no password it was not given.

201.description: Result; the `ok` field tells success from failure

get.summary: Read the LDAP configuration; the bind password is never returned

put.summary: Save the LDAP configuration; takes effect immediately

post.summary: Probe an LDAP connection without saving it

201.description: Result; the `ok` field tells success from failure

get.summary: Is a clock running, and since when
get.description: Answers {"running": false} when nothing is going. While one runs it carries startedAt, so a client can count up on its own rather than polling, and elapsedHours, which is what the entry would record - a browser with a wrong clock then shows a slightly wrong number and still books the right one.

post.summary: Start the clock
post.description: Body is optional: {"projectId": 3, "description": "..."}, both of which may be left out and settled later. Starting again replaces a clock already running - somebody who does that has changed their mind about what they are doing, and refusing would leave them to stop a clock measuring the wrong thing. To book the running clock first and carry on with something else, use /me/timer/switch. Always the caller's own clock; there is no route for anybody else's.

put.summary: Correct when the running clock started
put.description: Body: {"startedAt": "2026-10-19T08:52:00Z"} for a moment with its offset, or {"startedAt": "2026-10-19T08:52"} for a time on the wall clock, which is read in the caller's own timezone. For somebody who started work before pressing the button. Earlier or later, but never after now (timerStartInFuture). A start more than a day back makes a clock that can only be stopped with an end time, like any forgotten one; moving it across midnight moves the day the entry will land on. Refused with noTimerRunning when nothing runs.

200.description: The clock with its corrected start

delete.description: The way out of a clock nobody meant to start.

post.summary: Stop the clock and book what it measured
post.description:
Creates an ordinary time entry through the same service a typed booking goes through, so it meets the same rules: the daily cap, the project having to exist, be active and be visible, the description length. The duration is the measured one, to the second and rounded to nothing. The entry lands on the day the clock was *started*, in the caller's own timezone - somebody who starts at half past eleven at night and stops after midnight worked that evening.

Body is optional. Without one the clock is stopped now. {"endedAt": "2026-10-19T17:30"} books it up to the time the work ended instead - for the clock somebody forgot - read like startedAt on PUT /me/timer: with its offset as given, without one in the caller's timezone. The end may not lie in the future (timerEndInFuture) or before the start (timerEndBeforeStart).

Refused when what was measured is less than the smallest bookable duration (discard it instead) or more than one entry can hold (timerTooLong, with the hours measured); a forgotten clock is booked by saying when the work ended. A refusal leaves the clock running, so the time is not lost to it.

post.summary: Book the running clock and carry on with something else
post.description: Body as when starting: {"projectId": 4, "description": "..."}, both optional. Books what the running clock measured up to now, exactly as a stop would, and starts the next clock at that same second, so the two entries meet without a gap. Checked before anything is written: the next project is held to the rules a start is, and a booking that would be refused leaves the running clock as it was and starts nothing. Answers {"booked": <the entry>, "timer": <the clock now running>}. Refused with noTimerRunning when nothing runs.

200.description: The entry booked and the clock now running

201.description: The entry booked and the clock now running

get.description: Answers {"items": [{"validFrom": "2026-10-19", "hours": [8, 8, 8, 8, 6, 0, 0]}], "before": [8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 0, 0]}. Each item is a week, Monday first, in force from its day until the next item's; items are earliest first. `before` is the week for the days before the first plan, and for everybody who has none: the daily target from Monday to Friday and nothing at the weekend. The overtime balance measures each booked day against the week in force on it, so a day the week leaves free counts every hour booked on it as overtime.

post.summary: Plan a week from a day on
post.description: Body: {"validFrom": "2026-10-19", "hours": [8, 8, 8, 8, 6, 0, 0]} - exactly seven figures, Monday first. Replaces a plan starting on the same day; the days before keep the plan that was in force then, so going part time does not rewrite last month. Each figure is between 0 and 24, and none may exceed your own daily maximum (targetOverMaximum).

delete.summary: Take back the plan that starts on a day
delete.description: Its days go back to the plan before it, or to the daily target where there is none. A day no plan starts on answers 404.

get.description: Answers {"items": [{"id": 3, "projectId": 7, "durationHours": 0.25, "description": "Daily"}], "totalCount": 1}, in the order they were saved. Each part is null where the template fills nothing in. A template only fills the booking form - nothing is ever booked from one on its own - so it needs the right to book your own time, and its project is asked about again when the booking is made: one that has closed since is refused there, as any booking on it is.

post.summary: Keep a booking you make often as a template
post.description: Body: {"projectId": 7, "durationHours": 0.25, "description": "Daily"} - any of the three, at least one (templateEmpty). Held to what a booking is held to: hours between 0.01 and 24, a description no longer than one, and a project you can book on (projectClosedForBooking; one you cannot see answers 404). Saving one that fills the form exactly like a template you already have answers with that one rather than keeping a second. At most 50 per person (tooManyTemplates).

delete.description: Somebody else's template answers 404, the same as one that does not exist.

get.description: Answers {"items": [{"day": "2026-10-14", "kind": "halfVacation"}], "totalCount": 1}, earliest first. Range as ?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD; the default is the calendar year today falls in, in your own timezone. At most 371 days (rangeTooLong). A kind is one of vacation, halfVacation, sick, flexDay (a day off taken from the overtime balance, which keeps what the day asks) and localHoliday (a holiday where you work that your state does not keep as a whole).

post.summary: Record the working days of a range as away
post.description: Body: {"from": "2026-10-12", "to": "2026-10-23", "kind": "vacation"}. Only the days your planned week asks something of are recorded - a fortnight of leave is its ten working days - and a day already recorded takes the new kind. A range with no working day in it is refused (noWorkingDays). Answers with the days recorded, in the shape GET answers.

delete.summary: Take back the absence on a day
delete.description: A day with no absence recorded answers 404.

get.description: Answers {"year": 2026, "entitlement": 30, "carriedOver": 2, "taken": 18.5, "planned": 4, "remaining": 9.5, "entitlements": [{"fromYear": 2025, "days": 30}]}. ?year=YYYY, by default the year today falls in, in your own timezone. entitlement is what the year gives: the latest entitlement from that year or before. carriedOver is what the year before left - more than it gave where leave was not taken, less than nothing where it was overdrawn - back to the first year an entitlement was recorded for, before which there is no account. A day of leave (see /me/absences) uses a day and half a day of it a half, counted only on a day that is worked: one the week planned for it asks something of, and no public holiday. taken is leave up to today, planned is leave after it, and remaining is what is left once everything planned is taken.

put.summary: Give yourself days of leave a year from a year on
put.description: Body: {"fromYear": 2026, "days": 30} - between 0 and 366 days, in force from that year until the next entitlement's. Replaces an entitlement from the same year; the years before keep what they gave, so what they carried stays what it was. Answers with the account of fromYear, in the shape GET answers.

delete.description: Its years go back to the entitlement before it, or to none. A year no entitlement starts in answers 404.

get.summary: Every day of a range: what was booked and what it asked
get.description: Answers {"from", "to", "days": [{"date": "2026-10-19", "booked": 6.5, "target": 8, "absence": "sick", "holiday": "whitMonday"}], "totalBooked", "totalTarget"} - absence only on a day one is recorded (see /me/absences), holiday only on a public holiday of the state you keep (see /me/holidays). counts says whether the day counts towards the overtime balance, by the rule the balance keeps, so a week drawn from these comes to its figure. Every day of the range is there, the ones with nothing booked included - unlike the overtime balance, which counts only the days somebody worked. What a day asks is the week in force on it (see /me/schedules). Range as ?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD; the default is the week, Monday to Sunday, that today falls in, in your own timezone. At most 371 days (rangeTooLong), which is a year drawn as whole weeks.

post.summary: Book one of your weeks like another
post.description: Body: {"from": "2026-10-12", "to": "2026-10-19"} - two Mondays, the week to copy and the week to copy it into. Each entry of the first is booked on the same weekday of the second, with its project, hours and description, but only on days of the second week that have nothing booked yet: a day you have booked is left as it is. An entry whose project no longer takes bookings is left out. Everything else is held to the rules a booking is - the floor, the description, the daily maximum counting what the copy itself puts on a day - and written all at once or not at all. Answers {"copied": 9, "hours": 38.5, "kept": 1, "closed": 2}: the entries written and their hours, the days left as they were, and the entries left out. A first week with nothing in it is refused (nothingToCopy).

get.summary: What your own recorded time adds up to
get.description:
Totals the caller's own entries: per day, per project and per activity, with the overall total. Range as ?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD, inclusive at both ends; the default is the first of the current month to today, worked out in the caller's own timezone.

Deliberately not the project report. That one is keyed on a project id, so it cannot express "every project" or "no project"; this one is keyed on the caller and needs only timesheets:read:own. Neither answers with anybody's hours but the caller's.

Two details a chart depends on. Every day in the range is present, including the ones with nothing on them: a chart drawn only from the days that have entries shows a full week where there were two working days. And the entries with no project are their own row with projectId null, because "not categorised" is an answer worth seeing the size of rather than a gap. The activities the descriptions name with a # - #meeting, #review - are totalled as tags, [{"tag": "meeting", "hours": 3.5}], most hours first, beside untaggedHours for what names none. An entry naming two counts towards both, so the tags can add up to more than the total. A tag starts where a word does and runs over letters, digits, - and _; one of digits alone, #123, is a ticket number and not an activity.

post.summary: Export an evaluation as PDF
post.description: Lays out what an evaluation screen is showing and hands it back as a PDF: the report, the statistics, or an overtime calculation. Everything in the document arrives in the request, including the chart, which is drawn in the browser and sent as a PNG data URI - the chart in the file is the chart that was on the screen, in whichever of bars, columns or pie was chosen. Nothing is looked up, so this needs a session and no permission beyond it: there is no data here to be allowed or refused.

400.description: The document is missing a title, or is larger than one document may be

get.description: Takes the same filters as the list - projectId, from, to and q - with the same scoping: whoever may read only their own entries exports their own, whatever they ask for.

parameters.name: lang
parameters.description: Language for the column headings and the values inside them, e.g. `de`. Unknown or absent means English. The importer reads a file in any of these languages whatever this was set to, because the heading row is skipped by position and translated values are recognised in every language.

post.summary: Import time entries from .xlsx
post.description: Creates entries; it never changes or replaces existing ones. Every row goes through the same validation, daily ceiling and project visibility as a single booking. Every row is reported either way: the ones that would be written and the ones that cannot, with the reason. Nothing is written while any row is refused - a file half imported leaves somebody looking for which half.

post.summary: Import projects from .xlsx
post.description: Rows are matched by name: a name that exists is updated, a new one is created, so importing the same file twice changes nothing the second time. Every row becomes a project of the importer’s own, which no colleague can see - there was a Category column and a shared kind, and neither remains. An empty cell leaves that value as it is. The status is only written where it differs, so re-importing an export holding an archived project does not walk into the rule that archiving is only allowed from `completed`; asking for a status change the rule forbids is refused in the preview. Every row is reported either way: the ones that would be written and the ones that cannot, with the reason. Nothing is written while any row is refused - a file half imported leaves somebody looking for which half.

get.summary: Export roles as .xlsx, a column per permission
get.description: Needs `roles:read`. Every permission the application enforces gets a column holding yes or no, rather than one cell listing them: a typo in a list is a right silently dropped, and nothing about it looks wrong until somebody cannot open a screen. The permission columns are not translated - a permission is an identifier, and the role editor shows it verbatim.

post.summary: Import roles from .xlsx
post.description: Creates and changes roles, matched on the name. Needs `roles:write`. A permission column is read by its heading rather than by position, so a file exported before a right existed still imports correctly; a heading naming a permission this application does not enforce is refused, because it means the file came from somewhere else. A system role may be described differently and nothing else - its permissions are what keeps the installation administrable. Every row is reported either way, and nothing is written while any row is refused.

get.summary: Whether the installation is in maintenance mode
get.description: Public, like the branding and for the same reason: somebody opening the page during maintenance should read the notice on the sign-in screen rather than watch requests fail silently.

200.description: The maintenance state and its notice

put.summary: Turn maintenance mode on or off
put.description: While it is on, everything but signing in and the settings themselves is refused, so an administrator cannot lock themselves out of turning it off again.

200.description: The state as it now stands

get.summary: What is waiting for a restart
get.description: Lists the stored settings the running process does not match yet. `startedAt` changes when the process does, which is how a client can tell a restart it asked for actually happened.

200.description: Pending changes and the start time

post.summary: Restart the process
post.description: Only where the platform can do it: the process replaces itself, which needs exec, so it is refused on Windows with a reason naming what to do instead. And only into a database that answers: the connection the next start opens - the stored one, or the environment's where none is stored - is probed first, the way the start probes it, because a start ends on one that does not answer and nothing would be left to put it right from. The refusal carries what the driver said as `detail`.

400.description: The platform cannot restart in place (`restartUnsupported`)

409.description: The database the next start would open does not answer (`restartWouldNotStart`); nothing was restarted

post.summary: What a directory synchronisation would do
post.description: Changes nothing, so an administrator can see which accounts and how many recorded entries a run would remove before committing to it.

200.description: The report a run would produce

post.summary: Synchronise accounts with the directory
post.description: Matches on the directory-side identifier rather than the mail address, so a renamed mailbox is not read as a departure. `aborted` carries the reason a guard stopped the run, and `abortCode` with `abortValues` the same reason for a client to put in its reader's language, as with any refusal.

parameters.name: confirmed
parameters.description: The account ids a preview proposed and somebody confirmed, comma-separated; empty for a preview that proposed nobody. Given, the run deletes exactly these or changes nothing (`syncDiffersFromPreview`), because it asks the directory again and the answer may have moved. Absent, the run is unbound and held by the deletion limit alone, as a scheduled run is.

get.summary: List what recent directory runs changed
get.description: The latest runs that removed or added an account, newest first, at most twenty: when each ran, whether somebody confirmed it against a preview (the schedule and a script that sent no list did not), how many accounts it removed, how many time entries went with them, and how many accounts it added. Nothing about whom: the people a run removed are the people the purge erases, and the log names them for as long as it lasts. The built-in administrator's, as running one is.
Behind the built-in administrator: the log carries email addresses, request paths and whatever a failing driver decided to print.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Only lines newer than this sequence number.

parameters.name: levels
parameters.description: Comma-separated, e.g. `WARN,ERROR`. Absent means every level.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring of the message. A whole trace - the `traceId` of a record, which is also the `X-Correlation-ID` of the response to that request - finds the lines that request wrote.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many lines at most; the newest are kept.

parameters.name: epoch
parameters.description: The `epoch` of the answer `since` was taken from. Sequence numbers start again with the process, so a position counted by a process that has since been replaced is answered from the beginning of the running one, with `restarted` set.

200.description: Log lines, the levels that exist, how many were dropped or passed over, and the `epoch` to send back with `since`

get.summary: What version is running, and whether a newer one exists
get.description: Answers on every deployment, and says which kind it is. `available` is the only field a button should key on: it means a newer version exists, it published a binary for this platform, this deployment is one where installing lasts, and it has not already been downloaded. `installable` is false in a container - a binary swapped inside one is undone by the next recreate, so the image is what gets updated there. `pending` names a version already on disk and waiting for a restart. A lookup that failed comes back as `problem` with a 200 rather than as an error: the release feed being unreachable is not this application being broken. Needs the rights the built-in administrator has, not merely settings:manage.

200.description: The running version and what is available

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

post.summary: Download and install the newest release
post.description: Downloads the release's binary for this platform, checks it against the SHA256SUMS published beside it, and puts it where this process's own file is. Nothing is written into place until the hash matches - this is code that will be executed as the application on the next start. It does not restart: replacing the file and replacing the process are separate acts, and Windows cannot do the second at all, so the answer says which case this is. Refused in a container and when the check is switched off.

200.description: In place; the answer says whether a restart is needed or possible

400.description: Already current, switched off, or running in a container

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

500.description: The download or the checksum failed

post.summary: Ask the release feed now, rather than waiting out the cached answer
post.description: The version card is built from an answer the application keeps for six hours, because the release feed allows an unauthenticated caller sixty requests an hour per address and every open card would otherwise spend them. That is right for a screen refreshing itself and wrong for the minute after somebody publishes a release, when the card states a version that was newest this morning. This asks the feed at once and answers with the same body as `GET /settings/update`, so the card can be drawn again from what comes back. It has a limit of its own - once every five minutes for the whole installation - and refuses with `updateCheckedRecently` and the seconds remaining, so the button cannot hand back the problem the cache prevents. A feed that will not answer is reported as `problem` with a 200, exactly as the GET does. Needs the rights the built-in administrator has, not merely settings:manage.

201.description: The running version and what is available, freshly asked

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

409.description: Asked too recently, or the update check is switched off

bearerAuth.description: A personal API token. Not subject to the CSRF check, since a browser never sends this header on its own.

sessionCookie.name: gtr_session
sessionCookie.description: A browser session. State-changing calls made with this must also echo the gtr_csrf cookie in the X-CSRF-Token header and come from this origin; calls authenticated by a personal API token are exempt. A call carrying `X-Background-Request: 1` is held to the session's lifetime and idle timeout like any other but is not counted as the session being used - the interface sends it on the checks it makes by itself, so that a screen left open is signed out by the idle timeout. Opening the event stream counts the same way.

csrfToken.name: X-CSRF-Token
csrfToken.description: The value of the gtr_csrf cookie, echoed back. Required alongside sessionCookie on POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.

DocumentTable.description: A set of figures as the screen showed them.

numeric.description: Which columns are set flush right. The interface knows, because its own headings carry a class saying so.

DocumentSection.description: One heading, with a chart and a table under it. Both are optional: the statistics screen is two charts and no table, and overtime is neither.

chart.description: A PNG as a data URI, beginning `data:image/png;base64,`. Anything else is refused - a URL would be this server fetching whatever address a request named.

subtitle.description: The period the evaluation covers, as the screen words it.

summary.description: The figures that stand on their own: a total, or the three numbers an overtime calculation comes to.
